claim: The actual read version is Cheah and Wang's 1998 IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation article, Learning Impedance Control for Robotic Manipulators. Here, learning means iterative learning over repeated finite-duration task executions: a feedforward control input is updated from trial to trial so that the closed-loop robot response converges to a prescribed target impedance, not neural-network training, reinforcement learning, or online discovery of the impedance parameters. A feedback controller and dynamic compensator maintain within-trial behavior, while the learned feedforward term reduces a reference-model or indirect impedance error across repetitions. Under the paper's gain inequalities, boundedness, smoothness, passivity, and task-space assumptions, the impedance error converges to zero; experiments on a three-degree-of-freedom SEIKO TT3000 SCARA report large error reduction across repeated free-contact-free operations despite unknown environment stiffness and contact location. The result advances fixed impedance toward repetitive-task refinement but remains tied to repeatability, a specified target impedance and reference trajectory, and restrictive convergence assumptions.
claim_locator: Actual read version: IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation, Vol. 14, No. 3, June 1998, pp. 452-465; Abstract and Section I; Section II, Eqs. 1-12; Section III, Eqs. 13-28 and Theorem with Remarks 3-6; Section IV, Figs. 1-11 and Eqs. 29-36; Section V Conclusion; Appendix proof, Eqs. 37-75.
epistemic_status: Full-text primary theory-and-experiment study of iterative learning impedance control. The convergence claim is theorem-supported only under the paper's stated system, gain, regularity, and repetition conditions; experimental trends are author-reported and were not independently reproduced. No conclusions are imported from other versions or from modern neural or reinforcement learning.
problem_and_setting: Conventional iterative learning controllers refine prescribed motion or force trajectories, whereas impedance control specifies a dynamic relationship between reference-position error and interaction force and may not provide separately known desired motion and force trajectories. The environment stiffness and unloaded contact position are assumed unknown, making direct construction of the desired contact force and position histories unavailable. The paper asks how a robot performing the same finite-duration manipulation operation repeatedly can learn the feedforward action required to reproduce a given target impedance across free motion, entry into contact, compliant contact motion, exit from contact, and subsequent free motion.
method_or_mechanism: The constrained manipulator is expressed in task space through a nonsingular Jacobian over a finite workspace. The environment is represented by a positive-definite linear stiffness relation with unknown stiffness matrix and unknown static contact position. A positive-definite target mass, damping, and stiffness define the desired impedance between reference acceleration, velocity, position error, and contact force. The controller combines a stabilizing feedback law, a strictly passive dynamic compensator with chosen gains, an intermediate state, and a feedforward learning input updated between operations by an iterative rule using an intermediate reference-model error. The impedance error does not appear directly in the update; the target relation is realized indirectly through compensator dynamics. The proof constructs desired but implementation-unknown state, force, and feedforward signals, uses passivity or small-gain arguments to establish bounded within-trial behavior and local Lipschitz properties, and defines an iteration-domain index function. A sufficient matrix and gain condition based on positive constants, norm bounds, and Lipschitz constants makes the index nonincreasing and forces the indirect model error, then the impedance error, to converge to zero for every time in the operation interval as the trial index tends to infinity.
content_summary: The paper reformulates iterative learning around a reference model rather than direct trajectory tracking. The repeated task has a reference trajectory, but successful learning is judged by whether the measured motion-force relationship matches the specified target impedance. This matters because unknown environment stiffness and contact position prevent prior derivation of separate desired force and motion trajectories. A within-trial feedback controller and strictly passive dynamic compensator provide stability, while a feedforward term is updated after each operation. The theorem gives sufficient convergence conditions through selected feedback and compensator gains and bounds on nonlinear robot terms; higher gains can satisfy the inequalities, and lightly damped targets or very stiff environments require higher controller gain because of larger overshoot. The method does not require force-derivative or acceleration measurement. In free motion, zero contact force makes convergence of impedance error also imply convergence of trajectory error. The same learning controller is retained across contact transitions. Hardware tests use a SEIKO TT3000 SCARA with one prismatic and two revolute joints, encoder-based position, differentiated velocity, an endpoint Lord force sensor, and a 244 Hz sampling rate. The repeated path includes free tracking, free-to-contact transition, compliant motion along a constraint plane, contact-to-free transition, and final free tracking. A steel ball reduces tangential friction. The first trial sets the learned input to zero and therefore provides feedback-only behavior. Across repeated operations, the reported impedance errors for all three joints decrease sharply, motion tracking errors decrease, and the contact-axis position error converges to a nonzero steady value consistent with impedance behavior under force rather than to zero. The authors also report convergence despite contact points changing across iterations, as reflected in the measured force. The paper does not learn the target mass, damping, or stiffness themselves; they are supplied as the desired model.
synthesis_role: Early variable-performance learning card showing the transition from fixed model-based impedance execution to trial-by-trial feedforward refinement of a prescribed impedance response. It establishes that the learned object can be the control input needed to realize a force-motion relation, rather than a force or position trajectory, and supplies a convergence proof and industrial-robot demonstration.
development_link: Classical impedance control required the programmer to specify both a target impedance and enough model knowledge for accurate realization. This work keeps the target impedance fixed but learns a repeatable feedforward control signal that compensates systematic robot and contact effects over successive executions, without requiring known environment stiffness or unloaded contact location. It unifies learning across free and contact phases without switching controllers. Relative to later adaptive and reinforcement-learning approaches, however, it does not select impedance online, generalize a policy across tasks, or explore uncertain contacts; its improvement is memorized along the repeated operation and depends on a prescribed reference, finite interval, stabilizing feedback structure, and convergence bounds.

evidence.statement: The paper explicitly defines learning control as iterative generation of a control action for a prescribed repeated operation.
The learning objective is convergence to a target impedance or reference-model response, rather than direct convergence to separately specified desired motion and force trajectories.
evidence.support_scope: Section I and Section II, Remarks 1-2.

evidence.statement: Environment stiffness and the unloaded contact position are assumed unknown, so the desired force and motion trajectories cannot be derived in advance from the target impedance.
The target impedance uses positive-definite mass, damping, and stiffness matrices and is defined over a task space whose Jacobian is assumed nonsingular in a finite workspace.

The control structure combines stabilizing feedback, a strictly passive dynamic compensator, and an iteratively updated feedforward input; the impedance error enters the learning mechanism indirectly through a reference-model error.

The theorem states that, under the specified gain choices and sufficient inequality involving nonlinear bounds and Lipschitz constants, the target-impedance error converges to zero at every time in the operation interval as repetitions increase.
evidence.support_scope: Section III Theorem, Eq. 23-24, and Appendix Eqs. 37-75.

evidence.statement: The stability argument uses the interconnection of a passive robot system and strictly passive compensator, alternatively a small-gain argument, to ensure bounded motion and regularity needed by the iteration proof.
evidence.support_scope: Section III and Appendix around Eqs. 40-48.

evidence.statement: The paper reports that higher control gains can satisfy the sufficient convergence inequalities, and that lightly damped targets or very stiff environments require higher gains.
The learning law does not require measurement or estimation of contact-force derivative or robot acceleration.
The experiment uses a three-degree-of-freedom SEIKO TT3000 SCARA with encoder position, differentiated velocity, endpoint force sensing, and 244 Hz sampling.
The repeated experimental path includes free motion, entry into contact, compliant contact motion, exit from contact, and final free motion under one learning controller.
With the learned input initially zero, the first operation is feedback-only; reported impedance and trajectory errors then decrease over repeated operations.

The contact-axis trajectory error converges to a force-dependent steady value rather than zero, while the impedance error converges, consistent with learning a relation rather than pure position tracking.
evidence.support_scope: Section IV-B, Fig. 8 and surrounding discussion.

evidence.statement: The authors report convergence even though measured contact points changed between iterations.

evidence_kind: Nonlinear task-space formulation, passivity- and small-gain-supported iterative convergence theorem with sufficient gain inequalities, and author-reported repeated-operation hardware experiment on one industrial SCARA; no neural-network training, reinforcement learning, statistical multi-task evaluation, or learned impedance-parameter policy.
boundary_conditions: The actual read source is the 1998 IEEE Transactions on Robotics and Automation journal version; only claims present in this file are included.
Learning is iteration-domain feedforward refinement over repetitions of a prescribed finite-duration operation, not continuous adaptation within a single novel task.
The target impedance and reference motion are supplied by the designer; the algorithm learns the feedforward input required to realize them, not the target mass, damping, or stiffness.
The manipulator operates in a finite workspace where the task-space Jacobian is nonsingular and joint-to-task mapping is one-to-one.
Robot inertia is symmetric positive definite, and the environment is modeled by a symmetric positive-definite linear stiffness relation.

The target inertia, damping, and stiffness matrices are positive definite, with additional symmetry conditions on matrix products used in the proof; diagonal choices are given as a sufficient practical case.
The theorem requires carefully chosen feedback, compensator, and learning gains satisfying a sufficient inequality involving norm and Lipschitz bounds; arbitrary gains are not covered.
Passivity or small-gain reasoning supplies boundedness of the within-trial interconnection; the iteration proof relies on local Lipschitz continuity and finite bounds of nonlinear robot terms.
The proof defines desired state, force, and feedforward signals that may be unknown and are used analytically rather than measured in implementation.
The environment stiffness and static position may be unknown, but the paper does not establish convergence for arbitrary time-varying, nonlinear, hysteretic, deformable, or active environments.
The same operation interval and prescribed action structure are repeated; generalization to dissimilar trajectories, durations, initial conditions, or tasks is not established.
Free-motion trajectory-error convergence follows as a special case when contact force is zero; during contact, nonzero position error can be the correct target-impedance response.

Higher gains proposed for lightly damped or stiff-contact cases may be limited in practice by actuator saturation, noise, sampling, and unmodeled dynamics, which are not incorporated in the stated theorem.

The experiment is limited to one three-degree-of-freedom SCARA, one path and contact-plane setup, one sampling configuration, and qualitative plotted convergence without reported confidence intervals or repeated-seed statistics.
Changing contact points observed in the experiment provide limited robustness evidence but do not constitute broad environment generalization.
The scheme avoids force derivatives and acceleration measurements but still uses force, position, and velocity information and a designed stabilizing controller.
assumptions: The user-supplied full text faithfully represents the accepted 1998 IEEE T-RA version despite extraction loss in many mathematical symbols.
The exact sufficient inequality is summarized structurally rather than reconstructed where OCR removed symbols; no stronger condition is inferred.
The operation index denotes repeated executions of the same prescribed task interval, and convergence is interpreted in that iteration index.

The paper's statement that exact dynamic knowledge is not required is interpreted as motivation for learning systematic feedforward action, not as proof of model-free operation under arbitrary uncertainty.
Experimental reductions in plotted errors are treated as author-reported evidence, not independent replication.
The term robustness is retained only as the authors' interpretation of convergence despite practical disturbances and varying contact points, not as a formal robust-stability guarantee.

reported: Conventional trajectory iterative learning cannot directly realize the desired impedance when environment stiffness and unloaded contact position are unknown and desired force and motion histories are therefore unavailable.
Separate learning controllers for free and contact motion require discontinuous switching at transitions.
Lightly damped desired impedance produces larger overshoot and requires higher feedback gain for the sufficient convergence condition.
A very stiff environment similarly requires higher controller gain.
The first feedback-only trial has substantially larger impedance error than later learned trials.
During contact, position error does not generally converge to zero because nonzero error is part of the desired force-motion impedance relation.
inferred: The learned feedforward signal can overfit a repeated path and may not transfer to different trajectories, contact geometries, speeds, durations, or initial conditions.
Trial-to-trial changes beyond the theorem's bounded regularity assumptions can prevent monotonic refinement or convergence.
Increasing gains to meet conservative bounds may excite unmodeled dynamics, amplify differentiated-velocity noise, or exceed actuator limits.
Unknown linear stiffness is tolerated indirectly, but nonlinear, discontinuous, or changing contact mechanics may invalidate the fixed target and convergence analysis.
Because target impedance parameters remain designer-selected, the method does not solve optimal or context-dependent impedance selection.
The convergence result does not by itself certify safe behavior on early trials before the feedforward input has learned the repeated interaction.
